segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Iconium the same thing happened: they went into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they spent a considerable time there, speaking boldly in reliance on the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders to be done through their hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the people of the city were divided: some were with the Jews and others with the apostles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When a move was made by both Gentiles and Jews, together with their leaders, to mistreat them and stone them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: they learned of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and to the surrounding region,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and there they went on announcing the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Lystra there sat a man who had no strength in his feet, lame from his mother’s womb, who had never walked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This man listened to Paul as he spoke. Paul looked intently at him and, seeing that he had faith to be healed,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Stand upright on your feet!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he sprang up and began to walk.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices and said in Lycaonian,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The gods have come down to us in human form!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because he was the one who took the lead in speaking.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood just outside the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates and, together with the crowds, wanted to offer sacrifice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men, why are you doing this? We too are human beings, with the same nature as you, and we are bringing you the good news that you should turn from these worthless things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In past generations he allowed all the nations to go their own ways.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good: he gave you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, and filled your hearts with food and gladness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even with these words they barely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium, and after winning over the crowds they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, supposing that he was dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the disciples gathered around him, he got up and went into the city. The next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After they had announced the good news to that city and made a good many disciples, they returned to Lystra, to Iconium, and to Antioch,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: strengthening the souls of the disciples and urging them to remain in the faith, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is through many afflictions that we must enter the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they had appointed elders for them in each assembly, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had come to believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after speaking the word in Perga they went down to Attalia,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been entrusted to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they arrived, they gathered the assembly and reported all that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they spent no little time with the disciples.

notes.traditional: they went together into the synagogue
notes.note: The Greek phrase can mean either “in the same way”—that is, as had just happened in Pisidian Antioch—or “together.” Older versions and some recent ones take it as “together”; others read it as here. Both fit the context, and the choice is not certain.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations,” and in the plural it was the ordinary Jewish way of referring to the non-Jewish peoples. It is rendered “Gentiles” here and in verses 5 and 27, and “nations” in verse 16, where all the world’s peoples are in view. It is the same word throughout.

Only here and in verse 14 does Acts call Paul and Barnabas “apostles”; elsewhere in the book the term is kept for the Twelve. The word meant an envoy sent on someone’s behalf, and many scholars think it is used here of the two as delegates sent out by the assembly in Antioch (13:1–3), though this is debated.

The Greek verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is now a religious term or a book title, so the plain sense is given here, as many modern translations also do.

The verb covers both physical healing and “being saved” in the fuller religious sense, and Luke often plays on the two. The immediate reference is to the man’s lameness, so “healed” is used, but a first-century reader would have heard the wider sense as well.

Zeus was the chief of the Greek gods and Hermes their messenger and spokesman, which is why Paul, as the speaker, is taken for Hermes. The Roman poet Ovid tells a story set in neighboring Phrygia in which Zeus and Hermes visit the region disguised as humans, which may explain the crowd’s reaction. Older English versions use the Latin names Jupiter and Mercury.

Tearing one’s garments was a Jewish gesture of grief or horror, used especially on hearing blasphemy. Paul and Barnabas react this way once they understand that they are about to be worshiped as gods; the delay is probably because the crowd had been speaking Lycaonian.

The word means empty, futile or useless, and the Septuagint uses it as a dismissive term for idols and foreign gods. “Vanities” now suggests conceit to most readers, so “worthless things” is used. The reference is to the gods and the sacrifice being prepared.

The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that presses on people. “Tribulation” is now often heard as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word does. Other versions have “hardships” or “persecutions.”

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The verb was used both of electing by a show of hands and, more generally, of appointing or choosing. Here Paul and Barnabas are the subject, so “appointed” is the natural sense. Whether the local believers had a part in the choice is not stated.

Two different cities named Antioch appear in this chapter. In verses 19 and 21 it is Antioch near Pisidia, in central Asia Minor. Here it is Antioch in Syria, the city from which Paul and Barnabas had been sent out (13:1–3).

candidates.reason: When used for fellow believers the plural recurs constantly across Acts and the letters, and translators split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers.”
The verb spans heal, rescue and save, and the Gospels and Acts often play on the overlap, so the split by sense needs a single policy.
“The word” as shorthand for the Christian message recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and versions vary between “word” and “message.”
Used for Jewish elders, community leaders and simply older men; “elder,” “presbyter” and “older man” need a consistent division.
The verb hovers between “disobey” and “refuse to believe” across John, Acts, Romans, Hebrews and 1 Peter, and versions differ verse by verse.
